A close reading for the week

“a sense sublime”

Lyrical Ballads · Tintern Abbey

Revisiting the river Wye after five years, Wordsworth measures what has died in him against what has replaced it. The exchange he records, raptures traded for a presence that rolls through all things, became one of the central ideas of Romantic poetry.

—I cannot paint
What then I was. The sounding cataract
Haunted me like a passion:1 the tall rock,
The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood,
Their colours and their forms, were then to me
An appetite: a feeling and a love,
That had no need of a remoter charm,
By thought supplied, or any interest
Unborrowed from the eye.—That time is past,
And all its aching joys are now no more,
And all its dizzy raptures.2

  1. 1

    Nature felt as appetite

    The younger self was “haunted” by the cataract, “like a passion”; he did not sit and contemplate it. Rock, mountain and wood were “an appetite”, a hunger more than a taste, needing no “remoter charm, / By thought supplied”: no ideas, no interpretation, nothing the eye did not deliver raw. The lines define a way of feeling so that the poem can announce its end.

  2. 2

    An elegy for intensity

    “That time is past,” he says, flatly, without cushioning. What died is named in two phrases, “aching joys” and “dizzy raptures”: pleasures so intense they hurt and unbalanced him. Wordsworth mourns them as one mourns youth, by listing what made it unbearable and calling the list a loss. Few poems admit so openly that growing wiser begins with growing numb.
